title: 9/11 in the Age of Unreality
author: Bethel McGrew
content:
![9/11 in the Age of
Unreality](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/09/IMG_4588.jpg)

The new Netflix production _Generation 9/11_ is one of those documentaries
that tries to do too many things at once, but it finds some of its most
affecting moments in interviews with the grown children of the dead. One young
woman, Laurel Homer, pays moving homage to her father, fallen United 93
copilot LeRoy Homer. As a Zoomer, she feels singularly lonely in her grief. To
the rest of her generation, the images of 9/11 are little more than irony-
pilled meme fodder. These are not like the memes that were circulated in old
email lists and printed out for preservation in the Library of Congress, the
ones photoshopping George W. Bush and his staff into action movie posters or
reshaping the Manhattan skyline as a middle finger. They're the kind that
depict Bush as Thanos making the towers disintegrate, or a pair of denim jeans
with a burning tower on each leg. Or, among the milder ones, Andrew Card
whispering in Bush's ear with a spoonful of baby food: "Another plane
incoming, sir."

Laurel stands apart from her peers, unable to participate in this ritual. Even
though she was too little to remember the day, her life has been indelibly
marked by it, marked by the Real. But her peers inhabit an age of unreality.

The September 11 attacks marked the last time America experienced a world-
historic news moment as a monoculture. The drama unfolded in real time on
television screens across homes and schools, bars and offices, holding the
country in spellbound horror. For children old enough to grasp what was
occurring, the images were forever carved into their memory. More than any
other cultural touchstone, it is the defining generational dividing line
between millennials and Gen Z, between the generation that can still remember
a world before YouTube and the iPhone and the generation that can't.
